Home / Heritage

The tree that named the town.

Ibaan is named for the Iba. The municipal heritage page records a tree that was once abundant here, became a symbol of the community, and is now locally rare.

The municipal page is written in Filipino. The English here is a summary, not an official translation.

What the page records

The town takes its name from the Iba tree. The municipal heritage page records a tree that was once abundant here, gave the town its identity, and is now locally rare.

Local name
Iba
English name
Malay Gooseberry
Compared to
kalamyas (bilimbi)
Location
Vicinity of Ibaan

Source: Municipality of Ibaan · Iba Tree heritage page ↗

Five things to notice.

These are the observations on the municipal heritage page, kept close to the original wording. The page describes the flower, leaf, fruit, scent, and kitchen uses.

  1. 1

    Flower

    Small flowers grow in tight clusters directly on the branches. They are pale green to yellow and have no strong scent.

  2. 2

    Leaves

    Long, triangular leaves sit opposite one another on slender, flexible branches. The veins are clearly visible, and the shape is compared to kalamyas.

  3. 3

    Fruit

    Round fruit grows in dense clusters on the branches. It starts pale green and turns bright yellow-green as it ripens, with a sharply sour taste.

  4. 4

    Fragrance

    The page records no strong smell in either the flowers or the fruit.

  5. 5

    Uses

    The fruit is used to sour fish, and to make vinegar, wine, and sweets soaked in limewater.

Why it matters.

History

Local history connects the town name to the tree, which once grew abundantly in the area and became a symbol of the community.

Daily life

The fruit is part of local cooking and food traditions, including fish dishes, vinegar, and wine.

Livelihood

Products from the tree, including vinegar, wine, and seasoning, have provided income to some families. The fruit can also be made into sweets.

A tree that is locally rare.

The municipal page describes the Iba as locally endangered: few old trees remain, few residents plant or care for it, and the page notes that it is not found in neighbouring towns.

What put it under pressure

  • A lack of care in earlier years left few remaining trees.
  • Changing food preferences reduced everyday use of the fruit.
  • Land-use change removed places where the tree once grew.

What is being done

  • A municipal Iba planting programme has been carried out in every barangay, led by barangay officials.
  • The Rotary Club of Metro Ibaan and Klub Iba are named as partner organisations.
  • The Rotary legacy project “Iba-lik ang Kasaysayan” aims to rebuild the tree population and reintroduce it to Ibaan residents.

“Iba-lik ang Kasaysayan”

The name of the Rotary Club of Metro Ibaan’s legacy project. The municipal page describes it as an effort to rebuild the tree population and reintroduce the Iba to Ibaan residents.

What the page does not say

The municipal page does not give a tree count or a survey of remaining trees. This guide does not invent one. It also does not repeat the page’s national conservation programme section, which is broader than Ibaan.

Read the source

The full entry, including the Filipino text and the municipality’s photographs, is on the official Ibaan website.
